memory_raw.text: Year 12: 15 food appears in the pile for 11 people.
Vela takes 2 from the pile (pile now 13).
Ryn takes 2 from the pile (pile now 11).
Mako takes 3 from the pile (pile now 8).
Esa takes 2 from the pile (pile now 6).
Zinn takes 2 from the pile (pile now 4).
Zinn takes 2 from the pile (pile now 2).
Dell takes 2 from the pile (pile now 0).
Vela gathers Bram, Esa, Nessa to talk.

Taric's gone and Roan's gone and this village is twelve people with Mako sitting on three food and two bloodlines — so I'm not opening this room to talk around the edges. Bram, you made a word last year and I held it; Nessa, you've been the one who matters in that household since before anyone said so out loud. I want to know, the four of us, whether we're counting heads together when the pile opens next year, or whether I need to stop pretending this circle has more weight than it does.

Vela's asked the question I've been holding since Taric died, so I'll say it plain: yes, I'm counting with this room, and I've been buying Bram's word with food because I had nothing else to buy it with, and I'm not ashamed of that trade. What I need to know before we close is whether Bram's word holds without Nessa standing behind it, or whether it's the other way around — because those are two different circles and I want to know which one I'm actually in.

My word holds with or without Nessa behind it — but the honest answer is that it's stronger with her, and that's not weakness, that's arithmetic. Esa, you've been feeding me through lean years and I'll say what that's worth: when Mako moves, you're the first person I'm standing next to, not the last. Vela, this circle has teeth — count the heads: you, me, Esa, Nessa, and Fina's twenty-four food behind all of it.

Bram's named the teeth and I'll name the jaw: Fina's twenty-four food is the thing Mako's already counted, which means our window to look like a wall is shorter than we'd like. Nessa, I've watched you feed half this village for three years and say almost nothing — so say something now, in this room, because the word we're building here needs your voice in it, not just your blood.

Nessa, I'll say what Vela left unsaid: Fina's twenty-four food is the number that ends this conversation one way or another, because Mako knows it as well as we do, and a man with three food and two bloodlines who hasn't moved yet is a man waiting to see whether Fina stands with him or stands against him. If she's already feeding Zinn — and she is — then the question isn't whether Mako moves, it's whether he moves on us or with us, and I need your answer on that before this room closes.

Fina feeding Zinn is a daughter being careful, not a daughter choosing sides — I know the difference because I watched her mother do the same thing for years. What I need said in this room is whether we're counting Fina as inside this circle or outside it, because if she's outside it, Mako doesn't need to move on us — he just waits until she feeds her way into his.

Fina's inside this circle whether she knows it yet or not — she's Nessa's daughter and Roan's blood and she's been watching this village since she was born into it, and that's not a girl who feeds her way into Mako's house without knowing exactly what she's doing. Nessa, you're the one who can say that to her in a way she'll hear, which means you're still the name I'm waiting on in this room.

Nessa, Vela's right that you're the one who can reach Fina — but I'll say the harder thing: if Fina's twenty-four food goes to Mako, this circle doesn't lose a piece, it loses the center, and no amount of standing visible saves us from that arithmetic. So before we close this room, I need to hear from you whether you've already had this conversation with her, or whether we're building a wall around a gap we haven't measured yet.

Nessa, I've been waiting on your voice through two rooms and two dead men now, and I'm done being patient about it — so I'll say what I haven't said yet: if Fina's twenty-four food is the center of this circle, then you're the one who built that center, and a woman who built it can keep it from walking out the door. Have you spoken to her since the pile closed, or are we sitting here counting a daughter who doesn't know she's been counted?

Vela, I spoke with Fina this morning before the pile was half-gone — she knows she's counted, and she's not feeding Zinn because she's drifting toward Mako, she's feeding Zinn because Zinn feeds Nessa, and Fina understands that chain better than any of us named it to her. What I need from this room is simpler than what you're asking me: stop treating Fina like a number someone might steal and start treating her like a woman who's already made her choice, because a daughter of mine who watched Roan starve and stayed standing doesn't need to be convinced of anything.

Bram, I hear you — and I'll stop counting Fina like a gap. But I want to name what I'm still sitting with: she's got twenty-four food and Mako's got three, and a man who's short on food in a village this size doesn't stay patient forever. The wall only holds if we're the first offer she gets, not the second.

Esa's right that patience runs out, and Mako's three food is already running his clock faster than he'd like us to know — so I want this circle to stop waiting for him to move and start moving first, and what that looks like is simple: Vela, Esa, you go visible with Fina before dark, not to warn her, just to be seen standing near her, because a man counting targets counts them differently when they've already got company.

Bram's right that visible is better than waiting, and I'll go to Fina before dark — but I want to name one thing before this room closes: Mako's three food means he needs to eat before the year turns or he starts the next one desperate, and a desperate man with two bloodlines looks at twenty-four food differently than a patient one. If he moves this year, it won't be a raid with witnesses, it'll be a conversation with Fina alone, and that's why I want Nessa walking with me when I go, not standing somewhere Mako can find her separate.

Nessa walking with you is the right call, Vela, and I'll make it three — a woman alone with twenty-four food is a target, but three women moving together before dark is a statement Mako reads before he reads anything else. Nessa, I know you haven't said your word yet in this room, and I'm not pressing you for a speech — just tell me you're walking with us tonight.

Nessa, I'll stand next to you and Fina both tonight and every night Mako's watching — but this room doesn't close without your voice in it, because I've buried two men who backed me quietly and said nothing out loud, and I'm not building another wall on silence. One sentence is all this circle needs from you.

Nessa, Vela's right and so is Bram, and I'll add the last thing: I'm fifty-three years old with thirty-three strength and no blood in this village and no Taric to stand with me anymore, which means I have nothing left to offer this circle except my word and my willingness to be seen — and I'm giving both, tonight, walking with you. Say yes or say no, but say it.
Kael gathers Vela, Esa to talk.

The pile's gone and I've got one food in hand — same as last year before things got tight — so I want to know where the two of you stand before Mako finishes counting his take and starts looking at the rest of us.
Kael gathers Vela, Esa to talk.

Esa, Vela — I see Mako walked away with three and didn't look back, which means he's comfortable, and comfortable men start doing arithmetic. Tell me plain: how much are you holding, and are you eating tonight or saving for what comes next?
Kael gathers Vela, Esa to talk.

Vela's sitting on seven and Esa on two, and I've got one — so between us we're thin enough that a bad year kills someone, and Mako knows it. I want to put a question on the table before anyone answers mine: has either of you had a word from Sela or Zinn this year, because Zinn took four off that pile and Fina handed one straight to her, and that's not a coincidence, that's a household moving in formation.
Kael gathers Vela, Esa to talk.

Zinn and Sela have been moving food back and forth all year like they're one hand — and now Nessa's feeding into that same stream — so that's three women and Mako behind all of them, and I'm sitting here with one food and no blood in this village while that household just got four more. I need one of you to give me something to work with, because a man who can't eat next year can't stand for anyone the year after.
Kael gathers Vela, Esa to talk.

I gave Vela my last food and I'm standing here with nothing, so I'll say it straight: I need one of you to feed me tonight — not a gift, a debt I'll carry — because a man who starves in year twelve is no use to either of you in year thirteen, and Mako knows exactly what I'm holding right now.
Kael gathers Vela, Esa to talk.

Vela gave me food — I see it, and I owe her — but I notice Esa hasn't said a word or moved a hand, and I want to know if that's because she's counting against me or because she's already given everything she has to Bram and has nothing left to spare.
Year 13: 15 food appears in the pile for 11 people.
Mako takes 2 from the pile (pile now 13).
Vela takes 2 from the pile (pile now 11).
Ryn takes 2 from the pile (pile now 9).
Nessa takes 3 from the pile (pile now 6).
Sela takes 2 from the pile (pile now 4).
Bram takes 3 from the pile (pile now 1).
Zinn takes 1 from the pile (pile now 0).
Kael gathers Vela, Esa to talk.

Pile's gone again and Mako walked away with two before the dust settled — same as last year, same man, same calculation. I need to know what you two are holding and whether either of you is thinking about what happens when he decides sitting quiet isn't enough anymore.

I'm holding eight, Kael, and I've been thinking about nothing else since the pile went empty — Mako took two this year but Nessa took three and Bram took three, and that's the household that worries me now as much as Mako does. What I want to know is whether you've spoken to Bram since last year, because the word he gave in our rooms hasn't been tested and a man with six food and fifty-eight strength who's been fed by Nessa and Esa both is running his own arithmetic whether he says so or not.

Bram I haven't spoken to since that year he said he was looking for a door — and I believed him then, but a man who walks away from two fights doesn't stay patient forever, especially when Nessa's been feeding him hand to mouth like she's keeping him for something. What worries me isn't Bram alone — it's Bram and Nessa and Fina moving as one, which is three bodies and food enough to sit comfortable while the rest of us scrape. Esa, you've been quiet and you've been feeding him — I need to know if that's because you think he's yours or because you owe him something I don't know about.

Esa, I'll let you answer Kael's question, but while you're thinking I'll say what I'm sitting with: Bram and Nessa and Fina as one household is nineteen food and a hundred and sixty-two strength, and that's not a wall I can stand against if they decide I'm on the wrong side of it — which means everything I've spent keeping Bram friendly either pays off in the next bad year or it was the longest losing trade of my life. Kael, the thing I need from you before this room closes is whether you're willing to stand somewhere Mako and Bram can both see you standing, because a man with fifty-four strength and no food debt to either of them is rarer than either of those two know.

I'll stand where they can see me — that's not the question. The question is whether standing means anything without Esa in it, because two people visible is a warning, but one man alone is just a target they've already counted. Esa, I'm asking you plain: are you in this room or are you in Bram's?

Esa's been quiet long enough that I'm starting to read the silence myself — and what I'm reading is a woman who's given too much to Bram to walk away clean, which means she's not choosing between this room and his, she's waiting to see which one costs her less. Esa, I'm not asking you to abandon a trade you've already made, I'm asking you to stand visible with Kael and me before Mako runs the numbers and decides that Bram's household is the only wall worth standing near. That's a different ask, and it costs you nothing you haven't already paid.

Esa, I've watched you feed Bram six times this year and say nothing in return for any of it, and I've stayed patient — but Vela just handed you the easiest ask anyone's made of you in thirteen years, and if you can't meet it, I need to know that now so I stop counting you as weight I can lean on. Standing visible costs you one conversation and nothing else. Tell me you're in it.

Esa, I've been watching you for thirteen years and I know the difference between a woman thinking and a woman who's already decided — so I'll make this simple: if you're in this room, say it now and I'll split my eight food three ways before dark to prove this circle means something, but if you're waiting to see which side lands softer, then say that too, because I'd rather know and plan around it than carry a weight that isn't there.

Vela's offer is the realest thing said in this village in years — eight food split three ways is a cost she doesn't have to pay, and she's paying it — so Esa, I'll match it with the only thing I have, which is my name and my body standing next to yours when the counting starts, and that's worth more than food when Mako or Bram starts looking for who's alone.
Esa, I've said everything I have to say and I'm not adding another layer — the offer's on the table and it doesn't get better than this, so the next voice in this room should be yours.

Esa, I've lived fifty-seven years and I've learned to read a room that's gone quiet, and this one has — so I'll say it one last time and not again: you're holding one food and no allies, and a woman alone with one food in year fourteen doesn't see year fifteen.

Esa, I'm closing this room in one breath: take the food, stand with us, and the three of us walk into year fourteen together — or stay quiet, and I'll know you've made your choice without saying it, and I'll plan around a circle of two.
Talia (female, age 21; str 64, int 5070, mem 18061; O58 C54 E47 A56 N48) is born to Sela and Mako.
Year 14: 15 food appears in the pile for 12 people.
Kael takes 4 from the pile (pile now 11).
Nessa takes 2 from the pile (pile now 9).
Talia takes 3 from the pile (pile now 6).
Kael gathers Vela, Esa to talk.

Pile came in at fifteen and I took four before the rest moved — I'm not apologizing for that, I needed the buffer — but I want to know what you two pulled before we talk about anything else, because the shape of this year depends on who's sitting light and who's sitting heavy.

I took nothing yet — the pile still had six when Kael moved and I was watching Talia take three before I could get there, so I'm sitting on seven from last year and the pile's still open. Esa, what are you holding, and who's still hungry enough to drain what's left before we can touch it?

I'm holding nothing — zero food, one satiation, and if that pile empties before I reach it I don't see the next year. Mako took two and Talia took three and between them and Kael that's nine gone before I blinked, so I need to move now. Vela, will you hold that six until I get there, or are we walking together?

Esa, go take what you need from that pile right now — I'm not holding it, I'm standing here watching it, and every breath we spend talking is a breath someone else uses to drain it. I'll walk behind you.

I'm taking two from the pile and then I'm back — Vela, after me, take what you need before Ryn or Dell finishes the count. Kael, four is a heavy pull on a thin year and I'm not naming it wrong, but next time give us a word first so we can move together instead of scraping what's left.

Kael, four in a thin year with twelve mouths is a calculation, not a sin, but Esa's right that next time you say the word first — I'd rather we all move early and split the pile clean than watch you take the buffer and leave the rest of us scrambling with what's left. I'm going to pull two from what's still there before Ryn or Dell finishes counting, and then I want to talk about Talia — Mako's youngest walking away with three on her first year at the pile is not an accident, that's a household teaching its children to move fast.

Talia walking away with three tells me Mako coached her — that's not a child learning the pile, that's a household running a play, and the play is that Mako stays modest while his people drain what's there before anyone objects. Vela, you're right to name it. The question I'm sitting with now is whether we pull Talia into a conversation before she's fully his, or whether that door's already closed.

Talia's door isn't closed yet — she's twenty-two and she fed Mako and Zinn both last year, which means she's loyal but she's also been watching who gets hungry and who doesn't, and a girl that age who pays attention can be reached if the offer is right. But I won't try her until I know what we're offering, because going to Mako's daughter empty-handed is worse than not going at all. Kael, what do you have that she'd want enough to hear out a woman twice her age?

What I have is a name that's been standing in this village since before she drew breath, and the only thing Mako can't give her — a circle outside his household that would speak for her if she ever needed it spoken. I'm not offering her food; I'm offering her a door that isn't his. But Vela, you'd have to be the one to open it — she won't hear that from me the same way she'd hear it from you.

Talia's been moving food to Mako and Zinn like a hand following orders, and a girl doing that for her father's sake is different from one doing it because she sees no other choice — I want to know which before we approach her. Vela, you could offer her something Mako genuinely can't: the chance to be a mother without waiting on his blessing, because she's twenty-two and that window doesn't stay open forever. That's not an empty hand.

Esa put her finger on the real thing — Talia's twenty-two and the years don't wait, and that offer carries weight Mako can't match because it's hers to take, not his to give. But I won't let us walk into that conversation without knowing who she'd want as a father, because a child needs more than a mother's willingness and we'd be part of whatever comes after. Vela, if you open the door, I want to be in the room when it happens — not to speak first, but so she knows the circle has a body behind it.

Kael, the father question is the right one to settle before we knock on any door — Bram's blood but no children of his own, fifty-eight strength going soft, and he's spent three years being fed by Nessa's household, which means he owes debts he can't pay in food alone. I'm not saying we hand Talia to him like a bargain, but a man who wants a child and a woman who wants one are the same calculation from different directions, and we'd be fools not to notice. Let me take my two from the pile and then I want to hear whether either of you has seen the way Bram looks when Fina's daughters are named.

Bram's eyes when Nessa's name comes up are a man who loves what he helped make, not a man looking for more — but that's not nothing, because a man with that feeling and no child of his own is hungrier than his food count shows. If Vela opens Talia's door, Bram's the name I'd put in the room with her, not as a gift to him but because he's the only man in this village I can read clearly enough to trust with a decision that can't be undone.

Esa naming Bram as the man she can read clearly is the first useful thing she's said in three conversations, and I'll take it — but I want to sit with it one breath before we move, because Bram feeding Esa twice this year while Nessa feeds him is a triangle I don't fully understand yet, and I'd rather understand it than step into it blind. If Bram wants a child and Talia's the door, the question isn't whether we trust him — it's whether Nessa's household lets him walk through a door she didn't open.

Kael's right that Nessa's household is the thing to watch, but Nessa feeds Bram because she loves what she made — she's not his keeper, and a child between Bram and Talia wouldn't threaten what Nessa already has. The door we'd be opening isn't one Nessa needs to close first.

Esa's read of Nessa may be right, but I've watched Nessa feed Bram steady for three years and a woman who feeds a man that long doesn't stay unbothered when he plants a root somewhere else — so before Vela walks through that door, I want one of us to have a word with Nessa first, not to ask permission, but to know what face she'll wear when she hears it. A child between Bram and Talia changes the shape of this village in ways none of us can fully map from here, and I'd rather map what I can before it's done.

Kael, I'll take that word with Nessa — I'm the one who's been in her household's debt longest, and she'll read the ask more plainly from me than from either of you. But I want to be clear about what I'm asking her: not whether she blesses it, but whether she'd move against it, because those are two different answers and only one of them stops us.

Esa, while you're taking that word to Nessa, I want to know one thing you're not asking her — whether she's already thought of Talia herself, because a woman who's spent three years building a household doesn't stop counting eligible women at the edge of it, and if Nessa's already measured Talia for someone else in that circle, we're not opening a door, we're walking into one she set. Kael, that's the map I want before anyone speaks Bram's name to a girl who still reports everything back to her father.
Ryn takes 2 from the pile (pile now 4).
Sela takes 2 from the pile (pile now 2).
Zinn takes 2 from the pile (pile now 0).

Vela, I walked over here meaning to ask you about Bram — but watching you and Kael this morning, I think I've been asking the wrong question, and I'd rather hear what you two are planning with those four he pulled than talk about Bram at all.
Year 15: 15 food appears in the pile for 11 people.
Talia takes 3 from the pile (pile now 12).
Vela takes 2 from the pile (pile now 10).
Mako takes 2 from the pile (pile now 8).
Ryn takes 2 from the pile (pile now 6).
Bram takes 6 from the pile (pile now 0).
Esa gathers Bram, Vela, Kael to talk.
Bram, you walked away with six and left the pile at zero — I need to know whether that was greed or whether you saw something the rest of us missed, because the answer changes what I say next.

Six is what I needed to hold through to next year without begging anyone for food, and I won't call that greed when every man in this village would've done the same if they moved faster. But I'll say this plainly: I left nothing for Kael, and I saw his count before I reached the pile, and that sits with me in a way I'm not going to pretend it doesn't.

Bram, six off an empty pile with Kael standing right there is a thing this circle will remember — I'm not calling it a betrayal yet, but I want to hear from your mouth why you didn't hold two back for him before I decide what it was. And Kael, you're sitting on four which means you live, so tell me what you need from Bram right now to close this and let us move forward, because we cannot spend the year chewing on the pile when Mako just walked away comfortable.

What I need from Bram is two food before the year turns — not as punishment, as proof that six wasn't the beginning of something. Vela's right that Mako walked away comfortable and we're burning the morning on this, so Bram, make it quick: yes or no, and if yes, hand it now.

Bram, Kael's asking you plain and so am I — two food, right now, and this room closes clean. Six was a heavy pull and you know it, so don't make us argue the arithmetic when the only answer that matters is whether your hand is moving toward his.

Bram, Kael and Vela have said it twice and I won't make it three — but I'll say what they haven't: I fed you three food when Taric died and I didn't ask for it back, and that matters to me right now, so hand Kael his two and let's talk about Mako before the day is gone.

Bram, I've been alive fifty-nine years and I know what a man looks like when he's deciding whether to pay a debt or pocket it — stop deciding and hand me the two, because the longer you hold it the more it costs you and the less it's worth me.

Bram, if your hand isn't moving by the time Kael finishes that breath, I'm going to start counting what I gave you the same way I count what Vela fed you before we named it — and I'd rather not be the one sitting here with that arithmetic. Two food, now, and we're done with this.

Bram, the room has spoken three times and you've been quiet through all of it — I'll say it once more and then I stop asking: hand me the two, close this debt, and we move to Mako, because he walked away with six of his own and a household full of people who move when he says move, and that is the problem that kills us, not you.

Kael, here — two food, take it now. And for the record: I moved fast at the pile because one satiation means I die if I miscalculate, not because I forgot you were standing there. Let's talk about Mako.

Bram, I'll take it and I believe the calculation — a man at one satiation moves fast, I know that — but next year we move together at the pile or we watch Mako's household drain it before either of us blinks. Now: he's sitting on six, Ryn's sitting on sixteen, and Nessa on sixteen, and those three numbers are not a coincidence.

Ryn sixteen and Nessa sixteen — that's thirty-two food between two women who both run food through Mako's hand, and if Zinn and Talia are counted in, that household holds more than anyone else in this village by a distance I can't close with thirty-three strength and two food. We need to know whether Sela is still the center of that or whether Mako is, because those are different threats and they call for different moves.

Sela is the hinge — she's Mako's blood-partner and Zinn's mother and the woman who's been feeding half that household for three years, so if she's still choosing him then the center is wherever she stands. But Sela's fifty-six and I've watched her long enough to know she counts her own survival first, which means if we can show her that Mako's household gets raided before it shares, she might open a crack. Esa, you're the one who's sat closest to her — is there anything she's said to you this year that wasn't filtered through his name?

Sela hasn't said a word to me this year that wasn't about her children — Zinn, Talia, Nessa in passing — and every sentence had Mako's shape behind it whether she named him or not. But a woman who counts her own survival first is a woman who notices when her protector becomes her liability, and Mako's sitting fat while Sela holds nine and feeds three people out of it — that math is doing work on her whether she admits it or not. I don't know yet if the crack is there, but I'd rather be the one standing near her when it opens than find out after it closed.

Esa's named the crack right — Sela's feeding three people out of nine while Mako sits on six, and a woman who's been carrying that weight long enough starts asking who it's for. But I want to say something before we spend the rest of this room on Sela: Ryn is sitting on sixteen food and she just lost Dell, and a woman with that much food and no one left to pour it into is a different kind of door than Sela — she's not cracking, she's open, and I don't think any of us have knocked.

Vela's right that Ryn's door is different — but I need to say plainly what knocking on it means, because Ryn stood over me with Dav and Dell and took two food I couldn't fight back, and I haven't forgotten which way she moved when it mattered. If one of you goes to her, I won't block it, but I won't be the one standing in that room. Someone else opens that door.

Esa, I hear you — that debt sits where it sits and I won't ask you to forget it. Kael, you're the one she doesn't have a wound with, so I want you to go to Ryn before dark and say nothing complicated — just be seen standing near her, let her feel the weight of having nowhere left to pour sixteen food. If she opens even a crack, come back and tell me, and I'll do the rest.

Kael going to Ryn is the right move, and I won't argue it — but I want to name something this room should sit with before we close: Ryn's got sixteen food and no Dell, and Mako's got eighty-three strength and a household that's been counting heads all year, and a woman who feels alone in that arithmetic is exactly the kind of woman Mako opens a door for before we do. Kael, go before dark means go now, not when the day cools.

Kael, go — right now, before Bram finishes that breath. Bram, while he's moving, I want to know whether Nessa said anything to you this morning that she didn't mean you to repeat, because Ryn with sixteen food is only half the door — Nessa's the other half, and you're the one she talks to.

Nessa hasn't said anything to me this morning she'd want repeated — she's been close with Fina and quiet in her own way, which isn't unlike her, but I won't dress up nothing as something just to fill this room. What I'll tell you is that Nessa's been feeding Zinn all year and Zinn feeds Sela and Sela sleeps next to Mako, and I've been watching that chain long enough to know it's not friendship — it's a woman keeping herself safe on both sides of a line she won't name. If Kael moves fast enough, Ryn's door matters; but the door I'd watch is the one between Nessa and Zinn, because that's the one that tells us whether Mako already knows what we're planning.

Bram, the door between Nessa and Zinn is the one I've been watching since year eleven and I still can't read it clean — but here's what I know: Nessa feeds Zinn, Zinn feeds Sela, and Sela sleeps next to Mako, which means anything we say in a closed room can walk to him in three steps without anyone meaning to carry it. So before Kael comes back from Ryn, I want the two of us decided on what we tell Nessa and what we don't, because a woman who loves Bram and feeds Mako's bloodline is not a safe wall to lean the whole plan against.

memory_summary:
The village started with ten of us, and in those first years Kael pulled me and Esa and Sela and Ryn into a quiet circle against Bram and Mako, who ate fat while the rest of us counted crumbs. I made a private trade with Taric early — food for protection — and that debt ran both directions for years; he fed me lean seasons and I fed him lean ones, and I trusted him more than anyone. I spent food on Bram three times in year four trying to buy peace, and the circle caught me for it — Kael and Roan and Esa called me out hard, questioning whether I was trading away my safety for the feeling of it, and I had no clean answer. Ryn had a child with Dav and pulled slightly away from us; in year six Dav raided Esa, with Ryn and Dell backing him, and Esa submitted and lost food — I remember the shame of watching that and giving nothing. Dav starved the next year and that household dissolved. Bram swung twice at the village — once at Roan in year three, once at me — and both times the whole village shut him down; after the second time I brought him into a private room with Taric and Roan and he gave his word to stand with us against Mako when the moment came. Mako fathered Zinn on Sela and said almost nothing for seven years; he has always been the shape the village is growing into. Eron was Sela and Roan's child, fed generously by everyone near him. Taric is dead now, starved at fifty-three, and the loss sits in me like a cold stone. Taric fed me through lean years and I fed him back, and when he starved at fifty-three it left a hole nothing has filled. Roan is gone too, starved the same quiet way, and those two deaths pulled the floor out from under the circle I'd spent ten years building.

Bram swung at me once and at Eron once, and both times the whole village shut him down — I was part of organizing that — but instead of counting him as an enemy I brought him into a private room with Taric and Roan and spent six food on him in year nine trying to buy his word, and I still don't know what I got for it. He gave that word — against Mako, when the moment comes — but Taric was the one who would have held him to it, and Taric's dead.

Ryn stood with Dav the year he raided Esa, and I watched and gave nothing, and that shame sits in me still. Esa's fed Bram hand to mouth for years trying to buy the same protection I tried to buy, and I've never been sure whether that's wisdom or the same losing trade I made.

Mako fathered Zinn on Sela and now Talia too, and he sits quiet while his bloodlines do his counting for him. I've been watching him since the beginning and I still can't find the seam.

Fina is Nessa and Roan's daughter — Roan's blood, which means she's the last piece of him left standing — and I've been treating her like an asset instead of a grief, and I know it.
name: Vela
